title: What a learning disability is (and is not)
blurb: Apply the three-part definition of learning disability and tell it apart from a specific learning difficulty, autism and acquired brain injury.
question: Leanne, 31, is admitted with appendicitis. Her sister tells staff Leanne 'has a learning disability'. Leanne went to a mainstream school, has dyslexia, works as a hairdresser and lives with her partner. Does she meet the definition, and what should the nurse do?

teach.body: Valuing People (2001) defines a learning disability as a significantly reduced ability to understand new or complex information and to learn new skills (impaired intelligence), with a reduced ability to cope independently (impaired social functioning), which started before adulthood, with a lasting effect on development. In plain English: the person finds learning and everyday life harder across the board, and this began while they were growing up. All three parts must be present.

teach.caption: A low test score on its own, or difficulty with one skill such as reading, does not meet the definition.

Key wording
Used for
rows: Impaired intelligence + social functioning, before adulthood
Arrested or incomplete development of the mind
teach.caption: MHA 1983 s1(4) continues: 'which includes significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning'.

teach.body: The Mental Health Act 1983 defines learning disability as 'a state of arrested or incomplete development of the mind which includes significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning'. It mirrors the policy definition: development, intelligence and social functioning. Its importance is legal: other parts of the Act (covered in the mental health law lesson) limit when a learning disability alone can justify longer detention.

teach.h: Learning disability vs specific learning difficulty
teach.caption: Mencap describes dyslexia as a learning difficulty because, unlike a learning disability, it does not affect intellect.

teach.body: Internationally the term is 'intellectual disability'. ICD-11 calls it a 'disorder of intellectual development': intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour both significantly below average, starting in the developmental period. In education law and among some self-advocates 'learning difficulties' is also used, so check what a label means for this person. Use person-first, respectful language: 'a man with a learning disability', never a diagnosis as a noun. A learning disability is lifelong, yet people keep learning new skills throughout life.

teach.h: Learning disability and autism are different
teach.caption: An autistic person with average intellect does not have a learning disability, though they may still need adjustments.

teach.h: Scenario: Leanne on the surgical ward
teach.body: Leanne's history shows average general ability and independent living: she has dyslexia, a specific learning difficulty, not a learning disability. The nurse speaks to Leanne directly, presumes capacity and asks what would help her, for example reading consent information aloud or giving her more time. Her sister's label does not change the law: Leanne makes her own decisions, and any support is offered because she needs it, not because of a diagnosis she does not have.

teach.text: Three classic mix-ups: 'learning difficulty' (dyslexia, intellect unaffected) is not 'learning disability'; an IQ score alone does not meet the definition without impaired social functioning; and impairment that starts in adulthood (brain injury, dementia) is not a learning disability, however similar the needs look.

items: Valuing People: impaired intelligence + impaired social functioning + onset before adulthood.
MHA 1983 s1(4): arrested or incomplete development of the mind, with significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning.
Specific learning difficulties (dyslexia) do not affect general intellect.
Autism and learning disability are separate conditions that can co-occur.
Lifelong, but people keep learning; use person-first language.

summary: You can now apply the three-part Valuing People definition and the MHA 1983 legal definition of learning disability. You can tell a learning disability apart from a specific learning difficulty, autism and an acquired brain injury, and respond to the person rather than the label.

A.q: A student nurse lists impaired intelligence and impaired social functioning as parts of the Valuing People (2001) definition of learning disability. Which third feature completes the definition?
options: Onset before adulthood with a lasting effect on development
A genetic or chromosomal cause confirmed by laboratory testing
An IQ score below 50 on a formal standardised assessment
A co-occurring physical or sensory impairment from birth
A.why: Valuing People defines learning disability as impaired intelligence and impaired social functioning which started before adulthood, with a lasting effect on development.

whyNot.1: Many people with a learning disability have no identified cause; a genetic diagnosis is not part of the definition.
whyNot.2: The definition sets no IQ cut-off, and below 50 would exclude everyone with a mild learning disability.
whyNot.3: Additional physical or sensory impairments describe PMLD, not the core definition.

A.q: A new support worker asks what 'impaired social functioning' means in the definition of learning disability. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Difficulty making friends and keeping close relationships
Difficulty reading, writing and spelling at school level
A reduced ability to cope independently with everyday life
Behaviour that other people find difficult in public places
A.why: Valuing People equates impaired social functioning with a reduced ability to cope independently, for example with self-care, managing money, travel and keeping safe.

whyNot.0: Friendships are part of life, but social functioning in the definition is the wider ability to cope independently.
whyNot.1: Literacy difficulty alone describes a specific learning difficulty such as dyslexia.
whyNot.3: Behaviour that challenges is not part of the definition and is often communication of an unmet need.

A.q: During handover a colleague describes a learning disability as 'a mental illness that should improve with the right treatment'. Which correction is most accurate?
options: It is a temporary delay that most children grow out of by adulthood
It is a lifelong condition affecting development, not an illness
It is a specific learning difficulty that mainly affects reading
It is a mental illness that usually responds to medication
A.why: A learning disability starts before adulthood and has a lasting effect on development. It is not an illness to be cured, although people continue to learn new skills with support.

whyNot.0: Children do not grow out of a learning disability; it is lifelong.
whyNot.2: That describes dyslexia, which does not affect general intellect.
whyNot.3: Medication does not treat a learning disability; people may have co-occurring mental illness that needs its own treatment.

B.q: A nurse who trained overseas reads that ICD-11 uses the term 'disorders of intellectual development'. Which statement about the ICD-11 description is accurate?
options: An IQ below 70 is enough without assessing everyday functioning
Onset may occur at any age if the impairment is permanent
Adaptive behaviour is measured instead of intellectual functioning
Intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour are both well below average
B.why: ICD-11 6A00 describes significantly below average intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour, originating during the developmental period.

whyNot.0: ICD-11 requires adaptive behaviour to be assessed as well as intellectual functioning.
whyNot.1: The condition must originate during the developmental period.
whyNot.2: Both are assessed together; adaptive behaviour does not replace intellectual functioning.

B.q: Zainab, 16, has a moderate learning disability and is preparing to move to adult services. Her mother asks whether the learning disability will 'come off her records' when she turns 18. What is the best response?
options: It will be reassessed at 18 and removed if her skills have improved
It will be renamed a learning difficulty once she leaves school
It is lifelong, so it stays, and adult services will build on her skills
It will be removed at 18 because the definition covers childhood
B.why: A learning disability is lifelong with a lasting effect on development. Adult services continue support and people keep developing new skills throughout life.

whyNot.0: Skills can grow, but the learning disability itself is lifelong and is not removed at a set age.
whyNot.1: A learning difficulty is a different thing (intellect unaffected); leaving school does not change the condition.
whyNot.3: Onset must be before adulthood, but the condition itself continues into adult life.

B.q: A referral letter says Jamie, 14, 'has a learning difficulty' and explains that he has dyscalculia. His general school progress is otherwise in the average range. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: A specific difficulty with numbers that does not affect his general intellect
A mild learning disability that affects every area of his learning
A severe learning disability described in education terminology
An early sign of a learning disability that will appear later on
B.why: Dyscalculia is a specific learning difficulty: it affects one area of learning and does not reduce general intellectual ability, so the learning disability definition is not met.

whyNot.1: His general progress is average, so general intellect is not impaired.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests severe impairment; the letter names a specific difficulty with numbers.
whyNot.3: A specific learning difficulty is not a precursor to a learning disability.

C.q: Leanne, 31, is admitted with appendicitis. Her sister says Leanne 'has a learning disability' and offers to sign the consent form. Leanne went to a mainstream school, has dyslexia, works as a hairdresser and lives with her partner. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ask her sister to sign the consent form as her next of kin
Assess Leanne's capacity because a learning disability is reported
Speak to Leanne directly and ask what support would help her
Refer Leanne to the learning disability liaison team before surgery
C.why: Leanne's history shows a specific learning difficulty, not a learning disability. She is presumed to have capacity (MCA s1(2)); the nurse talks to her directly and offers support such as reading information aloud.

whyNot.0: Being next of kin gives her sister no power to consent for an adult, and Leanne is presumed to have capacity to give her own consent.
whyNot.1: Capacity is presumed (s1(2)) and cannot be judged lacking merely because of a condition (s2(3)); here the reported diagnosis is not even accurate.
whyNot.3: She does not meet the definition; the first step is to ask Leanne what help she wants.

C.q: A community nurse reviews four referrals. Which person most clearly meets the Valuing People definition of a learning disability?
options: Tariq, 20: low IQ and needs help with money and travel since childhood
Ruth, 35: low IQ measured during a severe depressive episode last month
Owen, 25: severe dyslexia and dyspraxia; lives and works independently
Nina, 30: needs help with self-care after a brain injury at age 26
C.why: Tariq shows impaired intelligence and impaired social functioning that began in childhood: all three parts of the definition.

whyNot.1: A score taken during severe depression, in an adult who coped before, does not show a developmental, lifelong impairment.
whyNot.2: Specific learning difficulties do not affect general intellect, and Owen lives independently.
whyNot.3: Nina's impairment began in adulthood, so it is an acquired brain injury, not a learning disability.

C.q: A tutor asks which phrase appears in the Mental Health Act 1983 s1(4) definition of learning disability. Which is correct?
options: Abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct
An IQ below 70 on formal standardised testing
Onset of the disability before the age of 18 years
Significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning
C.why: s1(4): 'a state of arrested or incomplete development of the mind which includes significant impairment of intelligence and social functioning'.

whyNot.0: That phrase is the separate qualifier in s1(2A)-(2B) that limits some detention powers; it is not part of the definition.
whyNot.1: The Act sets no IQ figure.
whyNot.2: The Act refers to arrested or incomplete development, not to a stated age.

reteach.title: Three keys to one lock
reteach.question: Think of the definition as a lock that opens only when three keys turn together. What are the keys, and what happens if one is missing?

blocks.h: Each key on its own is not enough
blocks.body: Key one: general learning is harder (impaired intelligence). Key two: everyday independent life is harder (impaired social functioning). Key three: it began while the person was developing, before adulthood. A low test score with good everyday coping misses key two. Dyslexia misses key one. A brain injury at 30 misses key three.

steps.label: Intelligence
steps.sub: General ability reduced, not one skill

steps.label: Social functioning
steps.sub: Help needed to cope day to day

blocks.text: If someone tells you a person 'has learning difficulties', ask what that means for them: it may be dyslexia (intellect unaffected) or it may be a learning disability described in education terms.

explain.body: A significantly reduced ability to understand new or complex information and to learn new skills. It affects learning generally, not one area such as reading.

test.q: Which description best fits the 'impaired intelligence' part of the definition?
options: Difficulty with spelling and reading speed
Reduced ability to learn new skills generally
Difficulty remembering names of new people
Poor results in one subject at school
test.why: Impaired intelligence is a significantly reduced ability to understand new or complex information and learn new skills in general.

whyNot.0: This describes a specific learning difficulty such as dyslexia.
whyNot.2: Forgetting names is common and does not show reduced general intellect.
whyNot.3: Difficulty in one subject points to a specific difficulty, not general impairment.

explain.body: A reduced ability to cope independently: self-care, managing money, travel, keeping safe and communicating needs. A person who manages everyday life independently does not meet this part, whatever an IQ test says.

test.q: Kai, 22, scored in the low range on one IQ test but lives alone, works full time and manages his own bills. Which part of the definition is not met?
options: Onset before adulthood
Impaired intelligence
Lasting effect on development
Impaired social functioning
test.why: Kai copes independently with everyday life, so impaired social functioning is not present and the definition is not met.

whyNot.0: Onset is not the issue in this scenario; his everyday coping is.
whyNot.1: A low score suggests reduced intelligence, but that alone is not enough.
whyNot.2: The lasting effect cannot be shown when everyday functioning is unaffected; the missing limb is social functioning.

explain.body: The impairment must start while the brain is developing (before, during or soon after birth, or in childhood) and affect development for life. Impairment from a brain injury, stroke or dementia in adult life is not a learning disability, though the person may need similar support.

test.q: Mr Davies, 52, has needed help with daily living since a stroke two years ago. His daughter asks whether he now has a learning disability. What is the best response?
options: No, because the impairment began in adulthood
Yes, because he now needs help with daily living
Yes, if an IQ test shows a reduced score now
No, because strokes affect movement rather than thinking
test.why: A learning disability must start before adulthood. Mr Davies has an acquired impairment from a stroke and needs support on that basis.

whyNot.1: Needing help is one part of the definition, but onset in adulthood excludes it.
whyNot.2: An IQ score after a stroke cannot meet the onset requirement.
whyNot.3: Strokes can affect thinking; the reason is the adult onset.

explain.body: Not a specific learning difficulty (dyslexia, dyscalculia, dyspraxia). Not autism, though the two can co-occur. Not a mental illness. Not an acquired brain injury. Each of these may still bring rights to reasonable adjustments.

test.q: Farah, 28, is autistic and works as a software tester. A ward clerk records 'learning disability' on her admission form. What is the most accurate correction?
options: Autism is classed as a mild learning disability
She is autistic but does not have a learning disability
Record a learning difficulty instead of a disability
Leave it, as autism and learning disability are linked
test.why: Autism and learning disability are separate conditions. Farah has no impairment of general intellect, so she does not have a learning disability, although she may need autism-related adjustments.

whyNot.0: Autism is not a form of learning disability; autistic people can have any intellectual ability.
whyNot.2: A learning difficulty is a different, specific condition and is not what Farah has.
whyNot.3: They can co-occur, but an inaccurate record can lead to wrong assumptions about her capacity.
